item.title: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketer
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2elpkg1l0jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketer - Published "You play with so many cricket stars. Why don't you take selfies with them?" Bilal Ahmad Dar once asked his young cousin, Auqib Nabi. Auqib smiled and replied: "One day I will reach a place where they will want to take selfies with me." Years later, that prediction has come true. On Monday, the 29-year-old all-rounder became the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to earn an India Test call-up after replacing Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the two-match series against Sri Lanka, which starts on 15 August. For a region where conflict, harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted sporting opportunities, Auqib's selection is being seen as a landmark moment. Raised in a small village in Baramulla district, Auqib grew up playing on local grounds with little infrastructure and few opportunities. His father, Ghulam Nabi Dar, a schoolteacher, initially wanted him to concentrate on academics and become a doctor. "There was no scope in cricket. We used to think playing sport was a waste of time, so I insisted that Auqib focused on his studies," Ghulam says. But Auqib's persistence eventually changed his father's mind. "After seeing his passion for cricket, I accepted it. I realised that, as a parent and a teacher, I shouldn't force him to do something he didn't want to do. I started supporting him." Auqib's childhood friend, Junaid Dar, remembers growing up in an environment where professional cricket barely seemed possible. "Auqib was obsessed with cricket from childhood. I used to ask him, 'Why are you doing all this? There's no future in it.' We came from a place where there was no concept of playing sport professionally and hardly any infrastructure." To pursue his dream, Auqib regularly travelled around 70km (43 miles) to Srinagar to practise on proper cricket pitches. He did not even own a pair of spike shoes when he attended his first cricket trials. But his work ethic never changed, his cousin Bilal says. "Auqib is very hardworking and consistent. He knows how to fight obstacles and make a way for himself. "He would wake up early to go to the gym and then practise for the rest of the day. He did that almost every day for 10 years." His breakthrough came in 2020 when he made his Ranji Trophy (India's top domestic tournament) debut for Jammu and Kashmir, taking a five-wicket haul against Jharkhand. Former India all-rounder Parvez Rasool, Jammu and Kashmir's first international cricketer and Auqib's long-time captain, says one quality always stood out. "I have followed Auqib's progress for a long time, and what stands out about him is his work ethic and discipline." Success, however, did not come overnight. Auqib claimed 44 wickets during the 2024-25 Ranji Trophy season, finishing as the competition's leading fast bowler, but remained largely outside the national conversation. "When you do well but don't get recognition, it hurts," his father says. "But we should never lose hope. Hope is what keeps the world intact. I always believed his time would come." It did. The following season, Auqib produced one of the finest bowling campaigns in recent Ranji Trophy history, taking 60 wickets in 10 matches to finish as the tournament's leading wicket-taker and help Jammu and Kashmir win their maiden Ranji Trophy title after a wait of 67 years. Those performances earned him an 84m rupees (£730,000; $982,000) Indian Premier League (IPL) contract with Delhi Capitals. Although opportunities in the IPL were limited, his red-ball exploits had already caught the attention of India's selectors. For Rasool, Auqib's Test call-up carries significance far beyond one player. "Playing Test cricket is the ultimate dream for any cricketer. It was my dream too. Seeing Auqib earn that call-up fills me with immense pride. "In a way, it feels like a dream many of us in Jammu and Kashmir carried has finally been realised through him. It is a historic moment not just for Auqib and his family, but for cricket across the region." He believes Auqib's journey is remarkable not just because he reached the Indian team, but because of where he came from. "Making it to the Indian team is incredibly difficult for any player, but the challenge is even greater when you come from Jammu and Kashmir. For years, we have had limited infrastructure, fewer opportunities and many obstacles that players from other parts of the country don't necessarily face. "To reach this level, you need exceptional consistency, mental strength and the determination to keep believing in yourself. Auqib has shown all of those qualities, which is why this achievement is so special." Jammu and Kashmir became affiliated with the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) in 1957, yet the region still has only two major cricket stadiums, both with limited facilities. Long winters, heavy snowfall and decades of conflict have further slowed cricket's development. "This is a landmark moment for cricket in Jammu and Kashmir," Rasool says. "For a long time, people questioned whether someone from our region could make it to India's Test team. Auqib has answered that question. His selection shows players from Jammu and Kashmir can compete with the best if they are given the opportunity." He believes Auqib's journey will inspire a new generation. "When I started playing, there weren't many role models from Jammu and Kashmir. Today, things are changing. "Auqib becoming the first player from the region to earn an India Test call-up will give countless youngsters the belief that they can dream big too. His journey proves that no matter where you come from or what challenges you face, hard work and perseverance can take you to the highest level." Back in Baramulla, Ghulam Nabi now finds himself recognised everywhere he goes. "People come up to me, hug me and say, 'This is Auqib's father.' "It makes me immensely proud."

item.title: Nigeria's mass wedding - and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7q17531do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nigeria's mass wedding - and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky - Published Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding. For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events. On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife. The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds. The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home. The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage. The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace. The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages. Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year. The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed. Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system. Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task. "Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC. He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer. The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple. According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies. Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage. All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations - including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility - before being cleared for the programme. Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results. In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme. Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria's struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year. "As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country's economy is not bright at the moment," he told the BBC. "This makes some people desperate to get on this list." One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said. Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago. One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list. "But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff," he said. He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August's wedding but he said he would try again next year. Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: "We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list." But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira. "We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples - all are covered by the government." One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him. "Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all," he told the BBC. His new wife is Aisha Auwal - the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes. Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was "very happy and can't wait to start a new life" with his customer-turned-bride. 24 year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi. Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah. "Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn't have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living." After Saturday's wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began. But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together. Watch: What we know about suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan Suspected cartel leader Daniel Kinahan has appeared in front of a special non-jury court in Dublin after an extradition treaty between Ireland and the UAE brought his 10 years of exile in Dubai to an abrupt end. Kinahan, aged 49, has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017. He has previously denied all charges against him. item.title: How Kinahan's hearing unfolded inside the courtroom in Dublin
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cly5zpx0ypdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How Kinahan's hearing unfolded inside the courtroom in Dublin Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appeared in court in Dublin on Sunday after being extradited from Dubai following his arrest there in April. Kinahan has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017. The 49-year-old was remanded in custody after appearing at the non-jury Special Criminal Court in Dublin, telling the court: " I think we all know I won't be getting bail." The Kinahan cartel has been responsible for trafficking tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world for more than 20 years, according to the UK's National Crime Agency. The BBC's Ireland correspondent, Chris Page, was inside the court during the hearing. Watch: Moment opposition MP throws eggs at Kosovo's acting PM An opposition MP, Time Kadrijaj, threw eggs at Kosovo's acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti during a plenary session on Saturday. The Alliance party MP hurled at least four eggs in Kurti's direction before lawmakers and police officers intervened. Chaos unfolded after Kurti told Parliament he needed more time to hold talks with other parties before proposing a candidate for speaker following the June snap election. Watch: BBC asks Infantino if he will resign as Fifa president The BBC has asked Fifa president Gianni Infantino if he has the support of football's South American governing body, Conmebol. The Fifa head has faced multiple calls to resign after his highly controversial attempt to sell private stakes in the World Cup, which he later abandoned. Infantino, who did not answer the BBC's questions, was in Colombia for the inauguration of the country's new President Abelardo de la Espriella. The BBC's South America correspondent Ione Wells later asked the Fifa president if he would step down.
